transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

It is very likely that your dryer is working normally. A heat-pump tumble dryer is essentially a fridge in reverse; it dries clothes using a refrigeration cycle rather than a hot heating element. Because of this, it naturally runs at a much lower temperature (so the drum feels only warm or barely warm) and takes significantly longer to dry a load—often 2 to 3 hours for a full batch—compared to an old condenser or vented dryer which blasts hot air and finishes in about 90 minutes. The fact that it is new and you are comparing it to the old machine suggests this is normal behaviour, not a fault. However, heat-pump dryers rely heavily on good airflow to work efficiently. If the filters are clogged with fluff, the cycle will take even longer than usual or leave clothes damp. Please check that the lint filter (in the door) and the condenser/evaporator unit (usually behind a flap at the bottom front) are clean and free of fluff. Also, ensure you aren't overloading the drum (it should be no more than two-thirds full) and that the towels weren't soaking wet from the washer. If those checks look good and the load was normal size, please let me know if the clothes come out dry at the end of the cycle, or if they are still damp.

Right, well I clean the fluff filters after every load and I cleaned the other filter at the bottom two weeks ago, it looks clean. The clothes do come out fully dry in the end, it just takes ages. Washer spins at 1000 rpm if that matters.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Since the filters are clean and the clothes do come out dry at the end of the cycle, your machine is probably working correctly. The 3.5-hour duration and the 'barely warm' feel are standard for a heat-pump dryer; it dries gently using recycled heat rather than blasting hot air like your old condenser model. The only factor that can make this process significantly longer is how wet the laundry was when you put it in. A 1000 rpm spin leaves quite a bit of moisture behind compared to higher speeds. If you find the cycle time unacceptable, try increasing your washer's spin speed (e.g., to 1200 or 1400 rpm) if the fabric allows; this will remove more water upfront and shorten the drying time. There is no fault here requiring an engineer or parts replacement.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
